subtitulo: Who did it doesn't matter — the passive
descripcion: The passive is not a more formal way of saying the same thing. It changes what the sentence is about. *They closed the plant* is about them; *The plant was closed* is about the plant. Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious, unimportant, or deliberately not mentioned — which is why it is everywhere in news and in technical writing.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: Forms and when to use it
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: **Use the passive when:** the doer is unknown (the samples were mislabelled), obvious (he was arrested), irrelevant (the results were published), or when the object is the real topic of the sentence. **Say who did it with by** — but only when it matters: The report was written **by the ministry**.

ejemplos.texto: *The targets have been missed three times.*
*Most of it can be recycled, but it isn't.*
*The plant is being closed at the end of the year.*
*Steps are being taken, according to the report.*

notas: Only verbs with an object can be made passive. *Happen*, *arrive*, *occur* and *die* have no passive form.
The passive without *by* is the normal case. Adding *by* every time makes writing heavy.
Don't write everything in the passive. Two or three in a paragraph is plenty.

es.en: Spanish usually avoids the passive and uses se instead: se recogen los residuos. English has no equivalent of that se, so where Spanish uses it, English normally takes the passive. That is why a Spanish speaker under-uses the passive in English and it sounds oddly personal.
es.es: El español suele evitar el pasivo y usa «se»: «se recogen los residuos». El inglés no tiene un equivalente de ese «se», por lo que normalmente usa el pasivo. De ahí que un hispanohablante use demasiado poco el pasivo inglés y el resultado suene extrañamente personal.

de.en: German uses the passive often, but its everyday alternative is man (Man hat das Werk geschlossen). The calque one closed the plant sounds odd in English, where the passive (the plant was closed) or a they-sentence is the natural choice.
de.de: Das Deutsche verwendet das Passiv häufig, aber die alltägliche Alternative ist «man» («Man hat das Werk geschlossen»). Die wörtliche Übertragung «one closed the plant» klingt im Englischen unnatürlich; natürlicher sind das Passiv («the plant was closed») oder ein Satz mit «they».

it.en: Italian often uses the si passivante (si raccolgono i rifiuti), which has no English counterpart. Italian speakers therefore under-use the English passive, although Italian venire (i rifiuti vengono raccolti) is a good bridge to the English process passive.
it.it: L'italiano usa spesso il «si» passivante («si raccolgono i rifiuti»), che non ha un corrispettivo inglese. Gli italofoni tendono quindi a usare poco il passivo inglese, anche se «venire» («i rifiuti vengono raccolti») è un buon ponte verso il passivo di processo.

fr.en: French often uses on (on a fermé l'usine) where English uses the passive, and the calque one closed the plant sounds odd. French speakers therefore under-use the English passive; the être-passive exists in French but is less frequent in speech.
fr.fr: Le français utilise souvent «on» («on a fermé l'usine») là où l'anglais emploie le passif, et le calque «one closed the plant» sonne étrange. Les francophones sous-utilisent donc le passif anglais ; le passif avec «être» existe en français mais est moins fréquent à l'oral.

pt.en: Portuguese often uses the se-passive (recolhe-se o lixo) or, in Brazil, a gente, where English uses the passive. Portuguese speakers therefore under-use the English passive, although the ser-passive (o lixo é recolhido) is a good bridge.
pt.pt: O português costuma usar a passiva com «se» («recolhe-se o lixo») ou, no Brasil, «a gente», onde o inglês usa o passivo. Por isso, falantes de português tendem a usar pouco o passivo inglês, embora a passiva com «ser» («o lixo é recolhido») seja uma boa ponte.

errores: Forgetting *be*: *The law passed in 2019* means the law itself did the passing.
Making an intransitive verb passive: *The accident was happened*.
Using the passive with no reason, which makes the text vague.

es: *se habla inglés* rendered as *Here speaks English* instead of *English is spoken here*.
de: *werden* rendered as *become*: *The house became built in 1990* instead of *was built*.
*von* rendered as *from*: *written from Goethe* instead of *by Goethe*.
it: Dropping the subject of the impersonal *si*: *In Italy eats pasta at lunch* instead of *In Italy people eat pasta* or *pasta is eaten*.
fr: *on* rendered as *one* everywhere: *One speaks English here* instead of *English is spoken here*.
pt: *vendem-se casas* rendered as *Sell houses* instead of *Houses for sale* or *Houses are sold here*.

traducciones.pt: Estão a ser tomadas medidas para…

mision.consigna: Write a short report about how a clothing company changed after criticism of its working conditions.
requisitos: five passive sentences in different tenses
one active sentence where the actor matters

microtareas.texto: Five active sentences about *online shopping*, then passive.
Three sentences with *has been* and *can be*.
Record 90 seconds: what *has been done* about *fast fashion*?

autochequeo: Does every passive have a form of *be* plus a past participle?
Did I make any intransitive verb passive?
Is there a reason for each passive, or did I use it by default?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the passive voice. (1) Mark each passive and check the form of *be* and the participle. (2) For each one, say whether the passive is justified or the active would be better. (3) Flag any passive of an intransitive verb. Do not correct anything else.
